title.en: Britain and America in the early 1960s

summary.en: Before the British Invasion, British pop mostly sat under American pop—but Britain had its own early pop practices.
summary.zh: 英伦入侵之前的英国流行乐基本处于美国流行乐之下，但英国人也有自己的早期流行乐实践。

body.zh:
现在让我们来看看，这段时期里英国的状况如何，究竟是什么导致了1964年美国的英伦入侵 (British Invasion) 。还记得吗，我在最初的课上强调过，这门课几乎是美国独家视角的摇滚史。但本节课是一个例外，我们要站在英国的角度来看摇滚史。另外从很多方面来看，英国视角的摇滚史，大不一样。英国地区的学生，对此最有发言权。所以，请勿因为我们常常谈及同一批音乐人，就轻易断定两者的情况也是一致的。有时也许正是两者的相似性，让我们忽视了一些重要、显著的差异。

以下就是1950年代末至60年代初英国的状况。若查看1963年之前英国的榜单，你会发现美国流行乐显然统治了榜单。具体而言，看看1961、62年间美国的热门单曲，再看看同期英国的各大榜单，你会发现两边大多是同一批唱片。其中多数唱片出自美国艺人之手，而非英国本土艺人。甚至是英国艺人，也在很多方面模仿他们的美国同行。我想，很多英国音乐人的心态或许是，他们的音乐不如美国音乐，但至少其是自制的本土产品。至于美国人的态度，我们很快也会讲到这一点，他们当然自认英国音乐不如美国音乐。当然，The Beatles和The Stones将会彻底改变这一局面。但眼下我想强调一个事实：即便是英国人也可能觉得自己的音乐不如美国。倒回二次世界大战期间，很多美国人来到英国，也将他们的流行音乐带到了这里；英国人大概就此成为了美国流行乐的爱好者。所以，最好的流行乐，对他们来说，就是美国的流行乐。

那些模仿美国艺人的人之中，相当一部分主要模仿的是Elvis Presley。英国最重要的模仿者可能就是Cliff Richard了。在1958年到1963年间，他一共有27首单曲登上英国的榜单。Cliff Richard很难在美国的榜单上闹出什么动静，但在英国他就像Elivs一样。我是说，他的歌曲一首接一首地成为热门。他是一个非常、非常成功的明星。英国也有他们的青少年偶像。我们在前一章讲到过，费城有一个叫Bob Marcucci的家伙包装出了很多年轻的青少年偶像。在英国，专事此业的人叫Larry Parnes。他管理着一大群青少年偶像，包括Tommy Steele、Marty Wilde和Billy Fury等。你能从这些艺名里可以看出来，这都是些大胆、令人兴奋的表演者。他们也推出了一首又一首的热门单曲。以上唱片对美国人来说基本是不存在的，因为他们从未见过这些唱片。这就是英国乐坛的一部分。所以如果站在英国角度来看这段时期，你就必须将以上事物纳入考虑。这就是The Beatles、The Stones及其他乐队让英国流行乐扬名于世之前面临的状况。

在60年代早期那些越过大西洋、成为热门的唱片之中，只有两张作品真正取得了巨大的成功。一张叫做《Telstar》，它是由The Tornadoes推出的一张器乐唱片，于1962年登上了英美两地榜单的首位。The Tornadoes其实是Billy Fury的伴奏乐队。Cliff Richard也有一个伴奏乐队，叫做The Shadows。The Shadows在英国也有一系列热门歌曲。那么，伴奏乐队The Tornadoes的《Telstar》在国际上或者说在美国成为了热门作品。有趣的是，它是由英国传奇制作人Joe Meek操刀创作、制作的；在很多方面上，他就是像是英国的Phil Spector。虽然，我觉得Phil Spector在美国取得的成就也许高于Joe Meek在英国取得的成就。不过，Joe Meek仍是一个早期的重要独立制作人。

同样，英国的唱片厂牌和电台也有一套相当不同的运作方式。这也使得英国乐坛在各方面都呈现出与美国相异的景象。关于美国，我们谈到过地区性电台的发展与电台播放音乐的方式，国内一直有大量的各式电台。这就为电台的专门化发展创造了契机，专门播放R&B、西部乡村乐、主流流行乐等流派的电台，不一而足。当然了，我们还有许许多多的唱片厂牌，独立厂牌的存在更是十分重要的。我们上次讲过，独立厂牌在推动摇滚乐走向大众的过程中起了多么重要的作用。但英国的情况很不一样。英国人只有BBC，他们自己在很多方面造成了这种局面；他们设立电台经营许可，要求电台与政府保持统一口径。所以，除BBC外再无可供收听的频道。你只能在BBC旗下的三个频道中选择，仅此而已。也有一个叫“卢森堡电台”的电台，在欧洲大陆上进行广播。还有些非法电台，设立在远洋的船只上，再向本土发回广播信号。问题就在于，像“卢森堡电台”这样的广播，编排节目时要向唱片厂牌付费。而谈到唱片厂牌，英国的独立厂牌真是寥寥无几了。这条路非常艰难，市场规模非常小，还被主流厂牌牢牢控制。既没有大量的电台可供自己的音乐走向大众，唱片商店的数量又很有限；我是说，在人口较少的情况下，许多唱片商人对于从独立厂牌中发掘唱片一事并不感兴趣。他们已经从主流厂牌那里拿到了很多的产品。这种状况让独立厂牌难以维系周转。这也意味着，英国人能听到的大部分所谓的摇滚乐其实经过了层层审核筛选，包括BBC 和那些主流厂牌。因此，他们能接触到的东西非常有限。我认为当时英国乐坛的多样性可能比不上美国，然而英国也存在着与我们不同的多样性，因为他们也有很多我们所说的不列颠艺人（British artists）。

英国流行乐坛发生过一场著名的早期运动，或者说它是一场于我们对60年代的讨论而言比较重要的运动——这场运动叫做Skiffle（译者注：一译“噪音爵士乐”，或“即兴摇滚乐”）。它由Lonnie Donegan领导发起，此人曾是一支爵士大乐队的成员。稍后我们还会谈到Trad Jazz（传统爵士乐） 。Donegan以美国民谣音乐作为改编的基础，同时加入一些大乐队的元素，还通过鼓的使用引入更为沉重的节拍；虽然有时他也会遵循传统，用刮板（washboard）作为敲击乐器。总之，他的版本的传统歌曲《Rock Island Line》在英国榜单登上了第八位，1956年时甚至在美国这边也拿到了排行榜第八的位置。这一类歌曲走红的现象在英国常常被称为skiffle craze。全英国的孩子们都购买了廉价的木吉他，学习弹奏第一把位的和弦，如G、C、D、Am、Em；同时也学习弹奏那些skiffle乐曲，这些曲子本质上是美国传统民谣的各种改编版本。这一切都发生在民谣复兴之前，美国的民谣复兴可以追溯到1958年或59年，而英国人于1956、57年时就已经在玩skiffle了。然而，这种由人人能弹的和弦和简单旋律组成的曲子，对The Beatles、The Rollings Stones还有Jimmy Page影响极大。事实上，你可以找到这么一个电视片段，当时还是个少年的Jimmy Page作为一名skiffle乐手现身某综艺节目，弹奏了一些skiffle音乐。因此，skiffle音乐非常非常重要。看看The Beatles在63、64和65年所做的音乐，我们可以从中找到skiffle的痕迹。

那时，英国还流行着别的东西。人们对所谓的Trad Jazz非常感兴趣。在英国，Trad Jazz更类似于——它和大乐队不太相像，当然也和bebop不太相像，而是更接近Dixieland的感觉。那种非常老式的新奥尔良爵士乐，正是Trad Jazz所追求的感觉。英国国内主打Trad Jazz的重要艺人包括 Ken Colyer、Chris Barber、Kenny Ball和Acker Bilk 。曾有两首来自英国的热门歌曲攻占了美国排行榜冠军宝座，一首是前文提到的《Telstar》，另一首叫《Stranger on a Shore》，正是出自the Acker Bilk orchestra之手。它在1962年登上了排行榜首位。所以谈到The Beatles实现的重大突破、他们手中的一系列冠军单曲时，也要知道他们并不是首支实现这一成就的英国乐队。不过当然了，The Beatles拿到的冠军更多，他们的成功也更长久。总之，以上大概就是Trad Jazz圈子的情况。

此外，英国还发生了一场运动，登上榜单的相关唱片不多，但我们能够确定参与者的身份：blues revivalists（布鲁斯复兴者）。像Cyril Davies、Alexis Korner和John Mayall这样的人都曾参与其中。谈及The Rolling Stones及其同类乐队——比如The Yardbirds和The Animals等——的根源时，这场运动就显得有些重要了。他们对美国的布鲁斯音乐非常着迷， 还尽力模仿演奏这些音乐。

那么，再想起这段时期，你会记得我们讲了skiffle、Trad Jazz和blues revivalists。这些音乐人也许是被二战期间远道而来的美国人迷倒了，于是也对美国文化中的所谓本土音乐十分着迷。这种着迷有时来自学历高、见识广的中产阶级，他们着迷的这些音乐却和最穷苦的大众最有关联，也和美国文化中最受压迫的元素最有关联。这是一种让人感到好奇的现象。我们没有时间去讨论其中的社会学意义，但它仍值得一提；因为对我们即将讲到的许多英国音乐人而言，这正是传统音乐之含义的根源。总之，如今我已给你速写了1963年之前英国的情形，下面就请将注意力转向The Beatles的崛起。
body.en:
Now let us look at Britain in this period, and what led to the British Invasion of America in 1964. Remember: early on I stressed that this course is almost entirely rock history from an American angle. This section is an exception—we take a British view. In many ways, rock history from Britain looks quite different. British students have the most to say here. So do not assume that talking about the same musicians means the situations match. Sometimes the similarities make us miss important, clear differences.

Here is Britain at the end of the 1950s and start of the 1960s. If you check British charts before 1963, American pop clearly dominates. Compare U.S. hit singles of 1961–62 with British charts of the same time: mostly the same records. Most are by American artists, not British ones. Even British artists often imitate their American peers. I think many British musicians felt their music was not as good as American music, but at least it was home-made local product. As for American attitudes—we will come to that—they of course assumed British music was inferior. The Beatles and the Stones would completely change that. For now I want to stress a fact: even the British may have felt their music was lesser. During World War II many Americans came to Britain and brought their popular music; the British largely became fans of American pop. So the best pop, to them, was American pop.

Among those who imitated American artists, a large share mainly imitated Elvis Presley. Britain’s most important imitator was probably Cliff Richard. From 1958 to 1963 he had 27 singles on the British charts. Cliff Richard rarely made noise on American charts, but in Britain he was like Elvis—hit after hit. He was a very, very successful star. Britain also had teen idols. In the last chapter we mentioned Bob Marcucci in Philadelphia packaging young teen idols. In Britain the specialist was Larry Parnes. He managed a stable of teen idols including Tommy Steele, Marty Wilde, and Billy Fury. You can tell from the stage names: bold, exciting performers. They too scored hit after hit. To Americans these records basically did not exist—they never saw them. That was part of the British scene. From a British angle you have to include it. That was the situation facing the Beatles, the Stones, and others before British pop made its worldwide name.

Of records that crossed the Atlantic and became hits in the early 1960s, only two really scored huge success. One was “Telstar,” an instrumental by the Tornadoes that topped charts in Britain and America in 1962. The Tornadoes were actually Billy Fury’s backing band. Cliff Richard also had a backing band, the Shadows, who had a run of British hits. So the Tornadoes’ “Telstar” became an international—or American—hit. Interestingly it was written and produced by legendary British producer Joe Meek; in many ways he was like Britain’s Phil Spector. I think Spector’s U.S. achievements may outrank Meek’s in Britain, but Meek was still an important early independent producer.

British record labels and radio also worked quite differently, so the British scene looked different from America’s in many respects. For the U.S. we talked about regional radio and how music was played—lots of stations of many kinds. That created room for specialization: R&B, country and western, mainstream pop, and so on. We also had many labels; independents mattered a great deal. Last time we saw how important independents were in pushing rock to a mass audience. Britain was different. The British had the BBC; in many ways they created that situation themselves—broadcast licenses required stations to stay aligned with the government. So outside the BBC there was little to hear. You chose among three BBC channels, that was it. There was also Radio Luxembourg, broadcasting from the Continent, and illegal stations on ships offshore sending signals home. The problem was that broadcasts like Radio Luxembourg had to pay labels when they programmed records. As for labels, true British independents were few. The path was hard, the market small, and majors held tight control. Without many stations to take music to the public, and with limited record shops—in a smaller population many dealers had little interest in digging through independents; they already got plenty from the majors—independents struggled to stay afloat. That also meant most so-called rock the British heard had passed layers of screening by the BBC and the majors. What they could access was very limited. I think British musical variety may have lagged America’s then, yet Britain had a different kind of variety, because they also had many British artists of their own.

A famous early movement in British pop—important for our 1960s discussion—was skiffle (sometimes glossed as “noise jazz” or “improvised rock”). Lonnie Donegan led it; he had been in a jazz big band. We will also mention trad jazz. Donegan adapted American folk, added big-band elements, and a heavier beat via drums—though sometimes he kept tradition and used a washboard for percussion. His version of the traditional “Rock Island Line” reached No. 8 in Britain and even No. 8 in the U.S. in 1956. Hits of this kind in Britain were often called the skiffle craze. Kids across Britain bought cheap acoustic guitars, learned first-position chords—G, C, D, Am, Em—and learned skiffle tunes that were essentially adaptations of American traditional folk. This was before the U.S. folk revival of about 1958–59; the British were already playing skiffle in 1956–57. Music built from easy chords and simple melodies deeply shaped the Beatles, the Rolling Stones, and Jimmy Page. In fact there is a TV clip of teenage Jimmy Page as a skiffle player on a variety show. So skiffle mattered a great deal. Look at what the Beatles did in 1963–65 and you can still find skiffle traces.

Other things were popular in Britain then. People were keen on so-called trad jazz. In Britain trad jazz was less like big band or bebop and closer to a Dixieland feel—very old New Orleans jazz. Important British trad artists included Ken Colyer, Chris Barber, Kenny Ball, and Acker Bilk. Two British hits topped the U.S. charts: “Telstar,” already mentioned, and “Stranger on the Shore” by the Acker Bilk orchestra, No. 1 in 1962. So when we talk about the Beatles’ breakthrough and their run of No. 1s, know they were not the first British act to do it—though of course they had more No. 1s and longer success. That roughly sketches the trad jazz circle.

There was also a movement with few chart records, but we can name the participants: blues revivalists. People like Cyril Davies, Alexis Korner, and John Mayall took part. When we talk about the roots of the Rolling Stones and related bands—Yardbirds, Animals, and so on—this movement matters. They were deeply into American blues and worked hard to imitate it.

So looking back at this period, remember skiffle, trad jazz, and blues revivalists. These musicians may have been dazzled by Americans who arrived during the war, and became fascinated with so-called vernacular music in American culture. Sometimes that fascination came from educated, well-read middle-class people, yet the music they loved was most tied to the poorest and most oppressed strands of American culture. That is a curious pattern. We do not have time for the sociology, but it is worth noting—because for many British musicians we are about to cover, that is the root of what “traditional music” meant. I have given you a sketch of Britain before 1963; next, the rise of the Beatles.
